title: Blush Placement for an Oval Face: Keep the Sweep Level, Not Up Toward the Temple

tables.section: Ten published guides for this shape, side by side
tables.caption: Oval-face blush placement as published, oldest first — four send it up toward the temple, two say outward and no more, one says keep it level and centred
head: Published
Where it appeared
Direction
The placement for an oval face, and what it warns against
rows: A makeup-discussion forum — one wearer's own account, not a brand guide

'I sweep my blush from my temple down in a parenthesis shape; it crosses down over the end of my cheekbone.' On her own long oval she reports the apples placement backfiring: it 'makes my jaw look weirdly narrow and accentuates my forehead.'
Byrdie — a beauty-editorial site, quoting a named artist

Highest point of the cheekbones, diffused outward horizontally — 'it's important not to over-blend blush toward the temples to keep the color centered.' The one guide of the ten that names the temple drag as the failure on this shape.

Very tops of the cheekbones, blended out toward the temples. Warns against low placement: 'Oval faces already have natural length, and a lower blush placement can end up dragging the features down' — the round-face warning, carried over to an oval.

'A soft sweep of powder blush works beautifully here. Keep the blending natural and seamless.' Its oval note is the one that matters: 'Because oval faces are already proportionate, you do not need heavy sculpting.'
Apples of the cheeks, blended up and outward toward the temples; the oval is to be flushed 'without altering proportions' — which is what the upward sweep then proceeds to do.
e.l.f. Cosmetics — a cosmetics brand's how-to blog
Start in the centre of the cheeks, pupils as the marker, then blend colour outward with an angled blush brush. No oval-specific warning.
Ulta Beauty — a beauty retailer's education hub
Directly on the apples, blended outward toward the hairline. The oval 'has the most flexibility'; the only instruction is to 'blend well so there are no harsh edges.'
Go-To Skincare — a skincare brand's guide
On the apples and along the cheekbones 'to enhance balance and harmony.' The 'avoid applying blush too high' warning on this page sits in the square-face section, not the oval one.
Flower Knows — a cosmetics brand's beauty guide

Apples blended outward, or 'slightly higher along the cheekbones and sweep toward the temples.' The oval is 'adaptable to a wide range of blush placements' — a chart by face shape, but no dates and no warning.
Focus on the top half of the cheeks, closest to the cheekbones. The oval gets the least specific advice of the ten: 'Any blush placement works for this face shape.'
tables.footnote: The date column is not one kind of date and which row is which should be stated. Four print a full dateline on the page — Byrdie '4 December 2025', Patrick Ta '23 January 2026', Charmacy '23 February 2026' and Laura Mercier '26 March 2026' — and those four are firm. Two carry only a footer copyright year, Ulta and Go-To both '© 2026', which dates the site rather than the article, so their place in the order is not firm. Three print no date at all anywhere — e.l.f., Flower Knows and Trinny London — and are grouped at the end for that reason rather than for any claim about when they appeared; Flower Knows does carry an on-page placement chart, but it is sorted by face shape and undated. The first row is the softest of all: it is a forum thread, and 2014 is the date the board was created, not the date this wearer posted, so it is here as a first-hand account and not as a dated guide. None of this changes any placement in the table. The 'Direction' column is the one to read down, and it does not split nine to one. Four rows send the colour up and out to a destination they name — Patrick Ta and Laura Mercier to the temples, Ulta to the hairline, Flower Knows to the temples. Two place the colour and say only outward, with no stop named — e.l.f. from the centre of the cheek at the pupil line, Go-To on the apples and along the cheekbones. Two carry no direction this column can read — Charmacy's 'soft sweep', and Trinny London's 'top half of the cheeks', which the same row then withdraws with 'any blush placement works for this face shape'. Two run the other way: the forum wearer sweeps down from the temple because the apples placement failed on her own long oval, and Byrdie says keep it level, keep it centred, and do not over-blend toward the temples. Of the ten, Byrdie is the only published guide that names the temple drag as the failure on this shape. The names are here so each row can be checked by somebody who is not us. No links are given to any of them.
